items.title: What If Earth Stopped Spinning?
items.description:
If Earth stopped spinning right now, you wouldn't stop with it. You'd keep flying east at up to 1,670 km/h, faster than sound at the equator. We stop the planet three ways: in one second, over a few decades, and the way it is really happening right now. Where would the oceans go? Why would one day last a whole year? And why are your days already getting longer?

Chapters
0:00 Earth stops. You don't.
0:41 How fast are we really moving?
1:16 How we know: Foucault's pendulum
1:43 Stop #1: in one second
2:58 The pole paradox
3:30 Stop #2: over a few decades
3:56 Where the oceans would go
4:36 A day that lasts a year
4:54 No more hurricanes
5:20 The Venus warning
5:54 Stop #3: the real slowdown
6:27 The Moon is drifting away
6:43 Leap seconds and melting ice
7:08 Will Earth ever stop?
7:35 What's next

Sources
- Esri ArcUser, Witold Fraczek, "What Would Happen If Earth Stopped Spinning?" (2010): equatorial bulge about 21.4 km, ocean bulge about 8 km at the equator, two polar oceans and an equatorial megacontinent, Chimborazo about 13,615 m above the new sea level, a day would last a year
- Astronomy magazine (Feb 2026), "What happens if Earth stops rotating?": equator moves at about 1,668 km/h; winds above 1,600 km/h in a sudden stop; leap seconds and a possible negative leap second in 2029
- World Meteorological Organization: highest recorded surface wind gust 408 km/h, Barrow Island, Australia, Tropical Cyclone Olivia, 10 April 1996
- NOAA / National Hurricane Center: tropical cyclones rarely form within about 5 degrees of the equator, where the Coriolis effect is too weak
- NASA Science, Venus facts: one rotation takes 243 Earth days, longer than its 225-day year; Venus has no intrinsic global magnetic field
- Winter et al. (2020), Paleoceanography and Paleoclimatology (AGU): 70-million-year-old rudist clam, 372 days per year, days about 23.5 hours
- Meyers and Malinverno (2018), PNAS (University of Wisconsin–Madison): 1.4 billion years ago a day lasted just over 18 hours; the Moon recedes about 3.82 cm per year
- Stephenson et al. (2016), Proceedings of the Royal Society A: length of day increasing by about 1.8 milliseconds per century
- Agnew (2024), Nature: melting polar ice is slowing Earth's rotation, delaying a possible negative leap second to about 2029; 27 leap seconds added since 1972 (IERS)
- NASA: the Sun will become a red giant in about 5 billion years; neutron stars: a teaspoon would weigh about as much as a mountain; fastest known pulsar spins 716 times per second
- Encyclopaedia Britannica, Foucault pendulum: Panthéon, Paris, 1851, 67 m wire; at Paris the swing plane turns about 11 degrees per hour; a full turn per day at the poles, none at the equator
- Own calculations (Python): rotation speed by latitude, spin energy (about 2.1e29 J, about 9 minutes of solar output), wind ratio

items.title: Top 5 Biggest Black Holes Ever Found 🕳️ #shorts
items.description:
The number one black hole on this list is 66 times wider than our entire solar system. Event horizons drawn to scale against our solar system and Voyager 1.

Sources
- McConnell et al. (2011), Nature: NGC 4889 black hole about 21 billion solar masses (Coma Cluster)
- Melo-Carneiro et al. (2025), MNRAS 541: Cosmic Horseshoe black hole about 36 billion solar masses, measured with gravitational lensing and stellar motions
- Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics / Mehrgan et al. (2019), ApJ: Holm 15A about 40 billion solar masses, direct stellar-dynamical measurement
- Shemmer et al. (2004), ApJ: TON 618 quasar, black hole estimated at about 66 billion solar masses
- Brockamp et al. (2016): Phoenix A, up to about 100 billion solar masses (model estimate, not a direct measurement)
- NASA JPL: Voyager 1 about 170 times the Earth–Sun distance, reaching one light-day in November 2026
- Own calculations: event horizon radius = 2.95 km per solar mass; light-day = 173 AU; Neptune's orbit about 60 AU across

Narration uses a synthetic voice. Visuals are original and drawn with code.
